finalArgument.thesis: The resurrection becomes the strongest explanation when early testimony, costly conviction, group claims, and the tomb are assessed together under an open supernatural prior.
premises: Jesus’s accepted crucifixion fixes a genuine death that any adequate explanation must connect to the rapid rise of resurrection proclamation.
Paul’s letters preserve early appearance traditions and his own transformative conviction close enough to the movement’s origins to constrain slow legendary accounts.
If a coordinated group encounter is historically established, private hallucination alone cannot explain why several people attributed one shared event to Jesus.
The debated empty-tomb considerations add conditional corroboration, although their force depends on source independence, burial confidence, and literary analysis.
A hypothesis gains comparative force when it explains otherwise diverse evidence with fewer independent auxiliary assumptions than its strongest rival.
finalArgument.conclusion: If those qualified premises survive source criticism, resurrection merits a serious posterior probability, though the debate does not show that it decisively defeats every mundane transmission model.

newArguments.title: Explanatory Coupling
newArguments.text: Suppose the creed, Paul’s conversion, and the bounded appearance sequence arose independently enough that a single early cause must explain all three. A resurrection predicts their shared personal referent and temporal concentration without requiring separate psychological triggers for each witness stream. The argument becomes genuinely stronger only if independence is demonstrated, because dependence would let one influential interpretation create the same apparent convergence.

newArguments.title: Costly Correction Test
newArguments.text: If named leaders repeatedly encountered informed opponents while preaching in Jerusalem, persistent proclamation could become evidence beyond mere sincerity: public contradiction should have supplied opportunities to correct easily exposed factual claims. This line requires proof about what opponents knew, what was publicly testable, and which exact claims leaders maintained; otherwise social commitment can explain persistence without confirming resurrection.

finalArgument.thesis: Historical restraint is warranted because the secure evidence primarily establishes early sincere belief and transmitted reports, not independently verified bodily encounters or an empty tomb.
premises: An early creed dates a claim but does not transform its compressed list into multiple accessible and independent eyewitness depositions.
Paul’s sincerity can be granted while the nature and cause of his experience remain underdetermined by his limited descriptions.
Collective profession can emerge through interpretation, memory convergence, and social reinforcement without a simultaneous shared hallucination or deliberate conspiracy.
Persecution supports sincerity only where a named knower faced punishment for the relevant assertion and possessed a meaningful opportunity to recant.
A low-frequency event requires evidence whose likelihood ratio over ordinary error is strong enough to compensate for its lower prior.
finalArgument.conclusion: Because the exchange leaves source independence, group phenomenology, martyr-specific recantation, and the tomb contested, withholding resurrection as the best historical conclusion remains rational without declaring miracles impossible.

newArguments.title: Compression Asymmetry
newArguments.text: Creedal compression can preserve a community’s stable conclusion while erasing differences among the experiences that produced it. Diverse dreams, visions, inherited reports, and interpretive memories may therefore appear later as one uniform list of appearances. This predicts formulaic agreement without requiring either coordinated deception or identical hallucination, and it shifts inquiry toward the pre-formula transmission process that the debate leaves largely unobserved.

newArguments.title: Posterior Ceiling
newArguments.text: When every major datum depends on a small, partially connected source network, adding correlated reports cannot increase confidence as though each were independent. The posterior probability of resurrection is therefore capped by uncertainty about that network’s reliability and dependence, even if each report is individually compatible with resurrection. The cap can be raised only through genuinely independent evidence whose expected presence differs sharply between resurrection and ordinary transmission.

noveltyMap.explanation: Synthesizes four qualified strands into a conditional Bayesian conclusion while explicitly retaining dependence and source-critical uncertainty absent from the closing rhetoric.
Develops a new independence-sensitive convergence argument from the temporal clustering of distinct witness streams rather than merely repeating the best-explanation claim.
Transforms the persecution exchange into a public-correction test with explicit conditions concerning opponent knowledge, testability, and the exact claims maintained.
Combines report-event distinctions, correlated testimony, person-specific sincerity, and probabilistic burden into a direct argument for historically rational suspension.
Introduces creedal compression as a mechanism by which heterogeneous experiences become a uniform appearance list without conspiracy or simultaneous group hallucination.
Derives a novel ceiling on evidential accumulation when apparently multiple reports share a small dependent source network and lack discriminatory independent confirmation.
